title: Franklin Expedition: How Were the Ships and Some Sailors Identified?
description:
What did an amended note, Inuit testimony and two changes of search route reveal about HMS Erebus and HMS Terror? Following the search in order, this episode separates the expedition's plans from the shipwreck discoveries and the identification of individual crew members. It reaches James Fitzjames in 2024 and the May 2026 identification of four more sailors, bringing the total to six. The ships' locations are known; the crew's complete final journey remains unresolved.

Sources checked: 2026-10-16. AI illustrations are narrative aids, not original records or exact reconstructions; named living people are not depicted as portraits.

chapters.greenland-parting: The ships freeze in the ice
chapters.return-to-note: A plan in the note's margin
chapters.new-account: An account points to a bay

h28b2255.text: It was May 1845 in Greenhithe, England. Two ships sailed out to find a route through the Arctic.

h2643cff.text: The supply ship returned. The 129 who went on with the expedition never returned to Britain.

h16d9247.text: Fourteen years later, searchers found a note with later writing and signatures.

hd8ce35d.text: Ten years later, an Inuit man pointed to a chart and drew where a ship had sunk.

he5a1f1d.text: Then, in 2014, a search team picked up a strange piece of iron onshore.

h81770de.text: Could these clues identify the ships and the people whose names were left on the note?

h3017f70.text: At Greenland, the supply ship returned with those leaving the expedition.

h3e67f13.text: When they sailed, the two ships carried 134 people. After the others went home, the 129 from our opening remained.

h69b3e42.text: Franklin led those who stayed. HMS Erebus and HMS Terror sailed west to seek the Northwest Passage.

h52abc08.text: Their first winter was near Beechey Island. They moved on when ice allowed.

hd476f23.text: But in their second September, sea ice trapped them off King William Island.

h159794c.text: A route west could still be drawn on a map, but the ships could no longer sail it.

h68ff78b.text: The next May, a party left the ships and wrote a report on their situation.

h7e65daf.text: On a naval form they noted their position and route. What else did they report?

h1dff7cb.text: It said, 'All well.' The date was May 28, 1847.

h0143711.text: Gore and Des Voeux wrote that first entry. Franklin was still in command.

h5cac1f4.text: The report stops on that day. What happened next appears in words added later.

hf598a9d.text: Another winter passed with the ships still trapped. But the number of people had changed.

h049dfec.text: When new words appeared on the same note, could the ships' mission still go on?

h72b4789.text: Words added the following year tell a different story: both ships were abandoned.

h851e868.text: The note dates the abandonment to April 22, 1848.

h323f98d.text: It says 105 people landed, now led by Crozier.

h1d74698.text: Franklin had died on June 11 the year before.

h882c0b9.text: The margin also records nine officers and 15 men already lost.

h421fbee.text: Crozier and Fitzjames signed the margin. Searchers now had to identify the people behind the record, too.

hb624337.text: The April 25 entry records a plan to head for Back's Fish River the next day.

h8de0bfd.text: So 'tomorrow' was April 26. The note records a plan, not a completed journey.

h7ca6f6b.text: Beyond the note, what had Inuit witnesses reported?

habe3055.text: Searchers had to ask coastal residents and piece together reports of the same expedition.

h1020a89.text: In 1854, John Rae noted Inuit reports: white men went south along King William Island's west coast.

hf9694ad.text: They also told Rae of bodies found near Back River's mouth.

h771e616.text: These accounts guided the search after the abandonment, but more evidence was needed.

hd7cc62f.text: Five years later, searchers found the amended note from our opening near Victory Point.

hfd3d3c2.text: Only then could they piece together part of the expedition's last stage. But where were the ships?

hef33fec.text: Searchers again sought people who knew this coast, asking what they had seen and heard.

h2c6f952.text: In Hall's 1869 inquiry, we meet the man who pointed to the map.

h3a137ee.text: His name was Inukpujijuq. He marked a wreck's reported location for Hall and drew a map.

ha4fd3dc.text: The location was near O'Reilly Island. Oral testimony had become a direction searchers could follow.

h7290bc7.text: Inuit interpreters helped make the account understood and the place recorded.

hef75ce9.text: That sketch could not be turned directly into modern seabed coordinates, but it offered a lead.

h673bff9.text: Later, researchers reexamined these accounts, comparing which ship was reported in which waters.

h82e96df.text: One was David Woodman, who published a study of Inuit testimony in 1992.

h2dea45a.text: Local researchers and guides helped searchers interpret place names and terrain.

h3369d03.text: Inuit accounts first narrowed the search area. What later clue on land shifted the underwater search?

hc2e7f24.text: The team searched not just underwater but for expedition objects onshore.

h8be50df.text: Sonar repeatedly swept the search area, flagging shapes worth a closer look.

h69509d0.text: Ice and weather limited where search vessels could sail that year.

he8d16a9.text: In 2014, weather focused more of the search farther south. First came an unexpected find on land.

h832761a.text: Remember the iron from our opening? On September 1, the team found it on a small island.

hc9c15f2.text: It looked a little like a bicycle fork. But this was on an Arctic shore.

h3630626.text: Comparing it with ship plans, researchers saw a part of a boat-launching device.

h725fbb3.text: They also found a wooden plug nearby, another ship part. The underwater search shifted.

h947eb54.text: The parts pointed offshore. But was there really a ship beneath those waters?

h852fd2d.text: The next day, sonar scanned the new area. Soon, the outline of a ship appeared on the screen.

h3153937.text: A ship's shape was not enough to name it. Searchers were looking for two ships.

h90ab1e6.text: They sent an underwater vehicle closer, then arranged a dive to inspect the hull.

h1c226ef.text: They compared its size, structure and identifiable parts with historic ship plans.

hbb9c913.text: This was HMS Erebus. After all those years, one of the ships finally had a name.

h3b4187b.text: Its location was near the site indicated in Inuit accounts.

h9ce4071.text: But one ship was still missing. Was HMS Terror nearby, or somewhere else?

h6db9312.text: Two years later, a crewman recalled something seen on the ice years earlier.

h66c7cde.text: His name was Sammy Kogvik. He said a wood-like object jutted from the ice in Terror Bay.

h7e8bbf3.text: The team turned toward that bay instead of following its original search route.

hdd8be47.text: An Arctic Research Foundation ship went into Terror Bay. On September 3, it found another wreck.

h1f855c2.text: Sonar showed the ship upright on the seabed. Then a remotely operated vehicle peered inside.

hf83594f.text: Some windows still held glass, and some hatches were shut. It was remarkably intact.

hcc5d7ed.text: Which features, beyond its state, could identify it?

h83aa802.text: The team compared underwater details with surviving ship plans.

h8533dbb.text: Parks Canada then sent divers to the site to confirm the find.

h540a29e.text: They checked two steering wheels and iron bow plating against plans.

h93d6e3d.text: On September 18, they confirmed the second ship: HMS Terror.

he2b2172.text: HMS Terror was not anchored. How and when it reached and sank in this bay remain unknown.

h4cb7289.text: The abandonment note records a plan to go south; the wreck marks a final location. The path between is missing.

h93c7c04.text: Remember Fitzjames, who signed the note? The ships had identifying structures; what could identify him?

h2fd7271.text: In 2024, researchers studied DNA from remains. They compared it with a living descendant's sample.

hf310a51.text: With genealogical records too, they identified the remains as Fitzjames. The signature now had a person.

h62e41a7.text: Research did not stop with Fitzjames. In May 2026, the team identified four more crew members.

h14bd2a6.text: That brought the number of identified expedition sailors to six.

h2a5e43b.text: Identifying someone's remains cannot fill in every step between leaving ship and dying.

hc9c673f.text: Remember the note from our opening? Other evidence has now linked one signature to a person.

h6980aac.text: Subscribe to the channel and join us as we follow verifiable records to solve strange cases.
